section_summary: This section examines whether and how Japan’s merchant marine should be rebuilt, including shipbuilding limits, overseas trade, calls at U.S. ports, and the effect on American and allied shipping. It includes State and Defense Department policy exchanges, a Defense staff study, and operational telegrams about bringing Japanese vessels into international service. The closing papers address seizures of Japanese fishing vessels and proposals for naval protection.

subfiles.title: Federation letter opposing immediate restoration of Japan’s prewar merchant fleet, with SCAP comments
subfiles.from: Frazer A. Bailey, for the Federation
subfiles.about: The Federation urges deferral of a four-million-ton Japanese merchant fleet while SCAP comments rebut its economic and security arguments.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion compares American and Japanese prewar shipping, disputes shipping’s value to Japan’s recovery, cites past subsidies, and argues for limiting Japanese ships mainly to domestic and nearby routes. SCAP’s inserted comments emphasize foreign-exchange savings, reject fixed trade-area limits, and support a phased, controlled revival of Japanese overseas shipping. The letter closes by requesting a chance to present further views to agencies considering the policy.

subfiles.title: Policy aspects regarding entry of Japanese merchant ships into United States ports
subfiles.from: C. V. Hulick, Office of Assistant Secretary of State for Occupied Areas
subfiles.to: Executive Officer, Civil Affairs Division, Department of the Army
subfiles.about: State supports eventual Japanese port calls but recommends interagency, congressional, labor, and industry consultation first.
subfiles.summary: Japanese calls at U.S. ports are consistent with economic rehabilitation, but their timing could provoke shipping and seamen’s opposition. Hulick proposes consultation through the Interdepartmental Shipping Committee before approval.

subfiles.title: Interim reply on Japanese shipping and shipbuilding staff study
subfiles.from: Walton Butterworth, Director for Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Robert West, Department of the Army
subfiles.about: Butterworth acknowledges an Army study and promises a response after State reviews it.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges the urgent policy question and defers a decision on the proposed working group pending consultation within State.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to Army study on Japanese shipping and shipbuilding
subfiles.to: Robert West, Department of the Army
subfiles.about: State reviews Army proposals for reviving Japanese shipping, ship construction, chartering, U.S. port calls, and policy coordination.
subfiles.summary: State supports restoring Japan’s merchant marine and export shipbuilding, subject to a Defense assessment of security limits. It opposes chartering U.S. war-built ships to Japan because of law, congressional resistance, and discrimination against wartime allies. The draft favors eventual Japanese calls at U.S. ports and recommends review by the Shipping Coordinating Committee before National Security Council consideration.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese vessel operations and reimbursement
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: State relays approval of an agreement on available Japanese vessels and notes funding and reimbursement issues.
subfiles.summary: Reports approval of the referenced agreement, directs activation of available vessels, and notes Treasury’s intended reimbursement request.

subfiles.title: Use of force to protect Japanese fishing vessels
subfiles.about: The memorandum reviews proposed U.S. naval patrols and Japanese-manned frigates to protect fishing vessels.
subfiles.summary: Moseley reports Defense’s request for a protest to China, a proposed regular U.S. naval patrol, and a plan to use returned frigates with Japanese crews. He weighs a prompt briefing for the Secretary against a fuller State objection in its reply to Defense.

subfiles.title: Preliminary comments on Department of Defense policy toward Japanese industry
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and Mr. Allison
subfiles.about: Fearey questions parts of a Defense study on Japanese industry, aviation, FEC papers, and treaty planning.
subfiles.summary: Fearey seeks clearer security limits on Japanese military facilities, questions proposed civil aviation and aircraft production, and corrects the claim that U.S. papers could be withdrawn unilaterally from the FEC. He favors addressing industrial policy during high-level treaty discussions.

subfiles.title: Comments on Defense proposals for the pre- and post-treaty eras
subfiles.about: Radius proposes State comments on unrestricted Japanese maritime industries and their international economic effects.
subfiles.summary: Radius accepts Defense’s security conclusion but warns that unrestricted Japanese shipping and shipbuilding could disadvantage Germany, European recovery countries, India, Pakistan, and U.S. operators. He anticipates congressional and labor opposition and possible retaliatory shipping preferences. He urges a unified government position through the Shipping Coordinating Committee and discussion with congressional committees.

subfiles.title: File memorandum on discussion of Radius’s shipping comments
subfiles.about: Hamilton records agreement to address Radius’s concerns at a Shipping Coordinating Committee meeting.
subfiles.summary: Participants agreed to let Defense explain its security view and raise maritime concerns in the committee.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum for Shipping Coordinating Committee file
subfiles.about: Hamilton asks Merchant to review the file before the committee meeting.
subfiles.summary: Requests file review and return of its tabs to Fearey.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Defense policy study on Japanese industry
subfiles.from: Carter B. Magruder, Department of the Army
subfiles.about: Magruder sends Defense’s industry study and Joint Chiefs’ response to State.
subfiles.summary: Transmits the study and military comments requested by State concerning post-occupation restrictions.

subfiles.title: Request for Joint Chiefs’ review of Japanese industry policy study
subfiles.about: Magruder requests a military review of an interservice study on Japanese industry.
subfiles.summary: Forwards the coordinated Army, Navy, and Air Force study to the Joint Chiefs for comment.

subfiles.title: Department of Defense policy towards Japanese industry
subfiles.to: Department of Defense and Joint Chiefs of Staff
subfiles.about: The study recommends security limits for civil aviation but no limits on Japan’s merchant marine, shipbuilding, or ship repair.
subfiles.summary: The study surveys U.S. and Far Eastern Commission restrictions, then argues that a prosperous Japan with access to long-distance transport serves U.S. security. It recommends no limitations on merchant shipping, shipbuilding, or ship repair, while limiting civil aviation to activity that does not threaten U.S. security. It also proposes changes to inconsistent occupation policy papers and asks the Joint Chiefs to review its conclusions.

subfiles.title: Joint Chiefs’ response on Japanese industry policy
subfiles.from: Omar N. Bradley, for the Joint Chiefs of Staff
subfiles.about: The Joint Chiefs find no military objection to the study’s principal conclusions, subject to security safeguards.
subfiles.summary: Endorses the relevant conclusions and reiterates the need to keep Japan aligned with Western powers and able to defend itself.

subfiles.title: Request for Defense views on Japanese non-armament industries
subfiles.to: Louis A. Johnson, Secretary of Defense
subfiles.about: Acheson asks what security restrictions should apply to Japanese aircraft manufacture and merchant shipping after occupation.
subfiles.summary: Acheson explains that new FEC proposals require a long-range security judgment. He reviews earlier Navy and occupation positions and requests specific Defense advice on aircraft, ship size and speed, shipbuilding capacity, and ships built for export or domestic use.

subfiles.title: Voorhees telegram on Japanese carriage of GARIOA supplies
subfiles.about: Voorhees reports legal clearance for Japanese ships to carry GARIOA supplies and urges gradual implementation.
subfiles.summary: Cites the Judge Advocate General’s view that the 1904 statute does not require U.S. ships for GARIOA cargo, while suggesting U.S. flag carriage for at least half and cautious trial calls at Gulf ports.

subfiles.title: MacArthur reply on readiness of Japanese ships for overseas trade
subfiles.to: Tracy S. Voorhees, Department of the Army
subfiles.about: MacArthur reports ship classification and conversion progress for Japanese overseas service.
subfiles.summary: Lists vessels ready or being converted for far-seas and near-seas trade, anticipates completing the conversion program in 1950, and promises help with finance and cargoes.

subfiles.title: State reply to Army study on Japanese shipping and shipbuilding
subfiles.to: Robert West, Department of the Army
subfiles.about: State gives detailed views on rebuilding Japanese shipping, ship construction, U.S. vessel charters, port calls, and interagency planning.
subfiles.summary: State endorses Japan’s merchant marine revival and ship construction for export and domestic needs, pending a security assessment of possible size and speed restrictions. It opposes chartering U.S. war-built vessels to Japan because of statutory, political, and diplomatic objections. It sees no law barring Japanese ships from U.S. ports and recommends consultation through the Shipping Coordinating Committee before a policy goes to the National Security Council.

subfiles.title: Request for Defense advice on a Japanese peace treaty
subfiles.to: Louis A. Johnson, Secretary of Defense
subfiles.about: Acheson requests Defense’s essential security requirements for a possible Japanese peace settlement.
subfiles.summary: Following exploratory talks with Bevin and a Cabinet discussion, Acheson asks Defense for military and security provisions that could shape a treaty draft. He stresses a tight schedule before Commonwealth consultations and proposes immediate joint drafting with a senior Defense planning officer.

subfiles.title: Measures to stop seizures of Japanese fishing vessels
subfiles.about: Butterworth reviews Chinese and Soviet seizures and proposed measures to protect Japanese fishing vessels.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports 67 seizures in 1948–49 and notes a U.S. protest to China. Butterworth considers a carefully controlled U.S. naval patrol if seizures continue, but raises FEC, Potsdam Declaration, and lend-lease objections to Japanese operation of returned frigates. He recommends signing a reply to Defense requiring advance State consultation.

subfiles.title: Routing slip for handling
subfiles.about: A file item is sent for handling following a telephone discussion.
subfiles.summary: Routes the item for handling after a call with Shaw and White.

subfiles.title: Handwritten note requesting policy clearance
subfiles.about: The writer seeks L and TRC views on a proposed U.S. policy response.
subfiles.summary: Requests consultation with L and TRC and a drafted acknowledgment; some handwriting is illegible.
